extracted.intended_audience: NLP/ML researchers and practitioners working on long-form story generation and evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and improving long-story (chapter-level) generation via the Next-Chapter-Prediction (NCP) task and verifiable reward modeling (VR-CLI), using human pairwise judgments, surface-level lexical metrics, and proxy automatic metrics across genres and model sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Next-Chapter-Prediction (NCP) task
rubrics_metrics.description: A story-generation task that uses a combination of high-level and locally relevant story information to predict the next chapter of a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design dataset/examples so that models receive both global (high-level plot/arc) and local (recent events, immediate context) story signals; evaluate generation quality by how well the model predicts a coherent next chapter given that information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable Rewards via Completion Likelihood Improvement (VR-CLI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reward modeling framework that allows optimizing a reasoning model to predict plans that increase the likelihood of the next chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train models (e.g., with GRPO) to produce plans/trace that demonstrably increase completion likelihood of a gold continuation. VR-CLI is verifiable because it measures likelihood improvement relative to a gold next-chapter; useful for optimizing reasoning models where such verifiability is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perplexity improvement as proxy metric (Improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Perplexity improvement correlates with human judgments." The Improvement metric (completion likelihood/perplexity improvement) can serve as a proxy for human preference judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute correlation with human judgments (Spearman's ρ reported: 0.33, p=0.01, N=60). Limitation: cannot be computed at true test time without a gold continuation, but useful for evaluating on unlabeled datasets where gold is available or for offline analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairwise human preference judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pairwise comparisons between story completions to determine which continuation is preferred by human annotators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect pairwise preference data (relative strength scores, preference probabilities) across models and settings; use such judgments as primary ground truth for generation quality. Break down preferences by model size and genre for deeper analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation dimensions (e.g., Creativity, Language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgments were collected along multiple dimensions; the paper explicitly mentions 'Creativity' and 'Language' as example evaluation dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report per-dimension preferences (e.g., annotators sometimes preferred Baseline-Reasoning in 'Creativity' and 'Language' for smaller models). Include dimension-level analyses rather than only overall preference to capture tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-level lexical metrics (length, word/trigram diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare generated chapters on length and lexical/trigram diversity to identify surface-level differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics like chapter length, word diversity, trigram diversity to detect superficial differences (e.g., SFT-based chapters were significantly shorter and less lexically diverse). Use these metrics to check whether annotator preferences are driven by content rather than surface artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotator bias / sanity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that annotators are not biased toward surface-level properties (e.g., longer/more lexically varied stories) and instead judge based on story content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check surface-level metrics (length/diversity) against pairwise preferences; if large surface differences exist but do not predict preference, annotator judgments are likely content-driven. Provide statistical tests and appendices with detailed tables to support this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific evaluation (percent improvement by genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure model improvements and preferences broken down by genre; the paper finds reasoning has the most pronounced effect on Sci‑Fi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report percent improvement and pairwise preferences per genre (tables for percent improvement, pairwise preferences by model size and genre). Use genre breakdowns to identify where reasoning/planning helps most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model size comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how reasoning and training methods affect different model sizes (e.g., 7B vs 3B): reasoning improves bigger models more; effects can be smaller or different for smaller models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run experiments across multiple model sizes, report relative strength scores and preference probabilities. Note that smaller models may favor different settings on dimensions like Creativity and Language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training-regime comparisons (SFT vs Baseline-Reasoning vs RL-Trained)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare outputs and human preferences across training regimes: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), baseline reasoning, and RL-trained reasoning variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report differences in length, lexical diversity, and human preference for each regime. Example finding: RL-Trained 7B variants outperformed baselines across most dimensions, while SFT-based chapters were shorter and less lexically diverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of expert judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Human judgments were collected from expert judges who evaluated story completions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer expert annotators (rather than naive crowds) for fine-grained chapter-level evaluation; report evaluator qualifications and ensure consistency/quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical validation of automatic metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: When using automatic/proxy metrics (e.g., Improvement/perplexity improvement), compute correlations and statistical significance with human judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report correlation coefficients (Spearman's ρ), p-values, and sample sizes to justify using automatic metrics as proxies for human evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: bias and harmful content mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that story-generation systems can perpetuate biases and produce harmful content; models trained on published books may inherit existing biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and mitigate biases in long-form generation; future work should develop methods to detect/mitigate stereotypical characters and harmful content. Be explicit about dataset sources and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics: intellectual property and dataset provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to avoid violating intellectual property rights of authors when using published books; dataset in this work cannot be publicly released because books were individually purchased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document dataset provenance (list books used), release code needed to reproduce experiments, and comply with IP constraints when sharing datasets/models.
